opus-5.5.text:
I think the frontier labs are, for very good reasons, building toward one model that's as general as possible: a single system that serves hundreds of millions of people and gets updated every few months. That's been incredibly powerful. But it means the model you talk to on day one hundred is basically the same model you talked to on day one. It doesn't really learn from you. Everything it knows about you lives in a context window or some retrieval layer bolted on the side, and that's a pretty thin form of memory.

Our bet is that the next big step is models that keep learning after deployment. They change their weights from experience, the way people do. If you think about what makes a great colleague valuable, it's not their raw general intelligence. It's that after six months they know your codebase, your preferences, the weird history of why things are the way they are. That knowledge is internalized, not looked up. We want models that accumulate that kind of expertise for a specific person or team.

So in that sense it's less "competing with" the frontier labs and more a different axis. They're pushing the base of general capability higher. We're asking what happens once you have a strong base model and let it specialize continuously to you. There are hard research problems in there: how to learn from sparse, messy interaction data, how to avoid catastrophic forgetting, how to do it efficiently enough that a model per person is actually feasible. Those problems don't get solved by scale alone, and I think that's where a focused effort can make a real difference.

Long term, I think the default experience of AI shifts from "a very smart stranger you consult" to "something that grows with you." That's the world we're trying to build toward.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the easiest way to put it is that the frontier labs are building one model for everyone, and we're trying to build a model for each person. And those sound like they might be the same goal, but they actually pull you in pretty different directions.

The frontier lab bet is essentially: make the model as capable as possible, and then personalization is something you layer on top. You put stuff in the context window, you retrieve some documents, maybe you have a memory feature that stores a few facts about the user. But the model itself is frozen. It's the same weights serving hundreds of millions of people. And that's a very reasonable bet if you think the bottleneck is raw capability, because then you want to pool all your compute into one giant training run.

Our view is a little different. We think a lot of what makes an assistant actually useful to a specific person isn't general capability, it's accumulated context. It's knowing how you write, what you've worked on for the last six months, which of your coworkers you mean when you say "ask Sam," the stuff you've already decided and don't want to relitigate. And the problem is that context grows without bound. You can't keep stuffing it into a prompt forever, and retrieval only gets you the parts that happen to look similar to your query. A lot of the most important things about you aren't things you'd ever retrieve, they're just background that shapes every answer.

So the Engram vision is that the model itself should learn from your experience. Your model's weights should actually be different from mine, because we've lived different lives, in the same way that two people with the same education still end up with very different expertise. The research question we care about is how you do that continually, cheaply, and without the model forgetting what it already knows.

I'd also say there's a kind of ownership angle that I think matters. If your assistant's knowledge of you lives entirely inside one company's frozen model plus their memory database, you're pretty locked in. If it lives in a model that's yours, that you can take with you, that's a different relationship with the technology. I don't think that's incompatible with what the frontier labs are doing. We're very much building on top of the base models they produce. It's more that we think the last mile, the part that makes it your model, is a research problem in its own right, and it's one that's kind of structurally hard for a lab to prioritize when their whole architecture is built around one model for everyone.

astra-6.text:
I think the distinction is between making one model more capable for everyone and making a model more useful for you. The frontier labs are largely pursuing general capabilities: how do you build a model that performs well across a huge range of tasks? Our vision starts with the individual. What would it mean to have a model that understands your context, learns from your feedback, and gets better at working with you over time?

Those approaches can be complementary. You want the capabilities of a strong foundation model, but you also want something that reflects your goals and judgment. So everyone having their own model doesn’t necessarily mean everyone training a frontier model from scratch. It means having an intelligence that adapts to you, rather than you continually having to explain yourself to it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the difference is really the unit you’re building for. The frontier labs are largely trying to build one model that’s very good at everything, for everyone. The vision of everyone having their own model starts with the individual: What would it look like to have a model that understands your context, learns from your experience, and gets better at helping you over time?

Those aren’t necessarily competing approaches. You’d want to benefit from advances in the underlying models. But there’s a different emphasis: intelligence isn’t just about how well a model performs on a general benchmark. It’s also about whether it understands what you’re trying to do, what matters to you, and how you work. The same answer can be great for one person and completely unhelpful for another.
